hero.headline: Judge orders Trump's name removed from Kennedy Center, halts closure
hero.body:
A federal judge has ordered that President Trump's name be removed from the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts and blocked the venue from closing for planned renovations.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled Friday that the performing arts center's board exceeded its authority when it voted to rename the institution. In his 94-page decision, Cooper wrote that it was "crystal clear" the arts complex has been named for the late President John F. Kennedy since 1964, when Congress officially redesignated it as the "John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts."

The ruling sided with Rep. Joyce Beatty, a Democrat from Ohio and an ex officio member of the center's board, who challenged the renaming. Cooper concluded the board lacked the statutory power to make such a change without broader authorization.

"The Court has concluded that the Board overstepped its statutory bounds by unilaterally renaming the Kennedy Center after President Trump," Cooper wrote in his decision.

The order requires the Trump administration to remove all signage bearing Trump's name from the building and to eliminate any references to a "Trump Kennedy Center" from official materials within 14 days. The decision takes effect immediately.

The ruling also blocks the Kennedy Center's planned closure later this year. The venue was scheduled to shut down so extensive renovations could begin, with programming expected to wind down over a two-year construction period.

The decision represents a significant setback to the administration's renovation plans for the performing arts venue. Trump had pushed for the changes as part of his broader vision for the facility.

The Kennedy Center, located in Washington, D.C., has functioned as the nation's cultural center since its opening. The building was designated as a living memorial to President Kennedy, who championed the arts during his administration.

Beatty brought the legal challenge in her capacity as a board member, arguing that renaming the institution violated the center's founding charter and federal law. The judge agreed with this assessment.

The order prevents any further steps toward closing the facility or advancing renovation plans under the current proposal. However, the ruling does not prevent Congress from potentially authorizing the renovation project or approving a different approach to the facility's future.

The decision comes after months of litigation surrounding the center's status and the administration's authority to make changes to the institution. Judge Cooper had previously signaled concerns about the board's actions during earlier proceedings in the case.

cards.headline: Trump meets advisers on Iran nuclear deal as negotiations reach tentative agreement
cards.teaser: President Trump held a meeting to make a final decision on a framework deal between the United States and Iran after negotiators reached a tentative agreement.
cards.body:
President Trump convened a meeting with his advisers following confirmation that the United States and Iran had reached a framework agreement. Trump emphasized that the Strait of Hormuz must be opened as part of any deal.

However, Trump did not announce a final decision on the proposed agreement during the meeting. He stated he would make his determination soon, with any deal requiring presidential approval before proceeding further.

cards.headline: Oil prices fall as U.S. and Iran move toward extending cease-fire
cards.body:
Oil prices dropped sharply as investors grew increasingly optimistic about a potential cease-fire extension between the United States and Iran. Brent crude futures, the global oil benchmark, fell 6 percent to $97.43 a barrel on Monday, marking the lowest level in two weeks as traders responded to signs that a peace deal could soon be finalized.

The decline reflects market expectations that resolving tensions in the Middle East could stabilize energy supplies and ease inflation concerns. However, significant obstacles remain. While negotiators have established a framework for an agreement, the two countries still disagree on critical issues, including Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for global petroleum flows. An Iranian government spokesperson cautioned that an agreement was "not imminent."

Warren Patterson, head of commodities strategy at ING, urged caution about the market's optimism. "We've been at this stage before, only for talks to break down. Therefore, the market will likely be more cautious about overreacting," he told Reuters.

Stock markets responded positively to the diplomatic developments, with Japan's Nikkei rising nearly 3 percent and the pan-European Stoxx 600 index climbing 1 percent. The movements suggest traders are cautiously balancing hopes for de-escalation against lingering uncertainty about whether any agreement will hold or what its terms might include.

Even if negotiations succeed, analysts warn that returning to normal energy flows will take considerable time. Infrastructure in Qatar and other regions suffered damage during the conflict, and repairs could take months. Current shipping data shows some progress, with two tankers carrying liquefied natural gas departing the strait on Monday and a supertanker carrying Iraqi crude leaving the Gulf after being stranded for nearly three months.

Giovanni Staunovo, a UBS analyst, emphasized that physical oil flows remain the key factor to monitor. "We continue to believe that the key factors for the oil market to watch should be the physical oil flows, and so far flows through the strait remain restricted," he said.

Despite Monday's decline, oil prices remain substantially higher than before the conflict escalated, when Brent crude traded around $70 a barrel. Barclays recently forecasted an average price of $100 per barrel for the year, though analysts note risks could push prices higher if talks stall.

Beyond energy markets, the potential agreement has broader economic implications. Higher oil prices have driven global inflation concerns and shifted expectations away from interest rate cuts toward rate increases. The dollar dipped 0.3 percent against major currencies on Monday, while gold climbed 1.46 percent to $4,574 an ounce. Stephen Innes, an independent analyst, noted that "treasury futures rallied, gold climbed and equity futures pushed higher as investors started pricing the possibility that the world's most dangerous energy choke point may soon reopen to something resembling normal flow."

cards.headline: Ukraine Prepares for Major Russian Attacks
cards.teaser: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the country is preparing for significant Russian military operations in the coming day.
cards.body:
President Zelenskyy warned that Ukraine should brace for significant Russian attacks within the next 24 hours, indicating Russia is preparing a new offensive operation in the region.

The warning reflects ongoing military tensions, with evidence suggesting Russian forces are positioning for intensified operations. A Russian drone launched during an overnight attack on Ukraine crashed into an apartment building in eastern Romania, injuring two people, according to Romanian authorities.

cards.headline: Bulgaria to end US military aircraft presence over visa dispute
cards.teaser: The Bulgarian prime minister said US military aircraft will leave Sofia at the end of June after visa program negotiations stalled.
cards.body:
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev announced Friday that his country will terminate the deployment of U.S. military aircraft in Sofia by the end of June. The decision stems from the Trump administration's rejection of visa-free travel for Bulgarian citizens to the United States.

Radev stated he had raised the visa suspension issue during discussions with U.S. officials. The dispute marks a significant disagreement between the two NATO allies over immigration policy.

cards.headline: UN Adds Israel and Russia to Sexual Violence Blacklist
cards.teaser: The United Nations placed both Israeli and Russian forces on its blacklist for sexual violence in conflict zones.
cards.body:
The UN added Israel and Russia to its blacklist for sexual violence in conflict, citing abuse by their security forces. The UN verified sexual abuse of 31 Palestinian men, women and children from Gaza and the occupied West Bank between 2023 and 2025. Israeli attacks included repeated gang-rapes and the use of sexual violence as torture, according to the report.

Russian forces were similarly cited for sexual violence in conflict zones. Both governments have blocked UN investigators from accessing their territories. The blacklist is part of the UN's annual monitoring of conflict-related sexual violence worldwide.

cards.headline: Wall Street indexes hit record closing highs on technology gains
cards.teaser: Major stock indexes closed at record levels, with technology companies leading gains and the Nasdaq rising 8% for May.
cards.body:
Wall Street reached new closing highs as technology stocks led the advance. The Nasdaq climbed 8% during May, while the S&P 500 extended its winning streak to nine consecutive weeks.

The market rally reflected investor optimism about technology companies and corporate earnings growth. Positive sentiment was further bolstered by hopes for a diplomatic agreement between the U.S. and Iran regarding Middle East developments.

hero.headline: Russian Drone Hits Apartment Building in Romania
hero.body:
A Russian drone struck an apartment building in the Romanian city of Galati during an overnight attack on Ukraine, according to Romanian authorities. The incident injured two people and sparked a fire that forced the evacuation of several residents. Romania is a NATO member state, and the alliance swiftly condemned what it called Moscow's reckless behavior.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance is "ready to defend every inch" of its territory following the strike. "Russia's reckless behaviour is a danger to us all," Rutte wrote on social media after speaking with Romanian President Nicusor Dan.

Romanian officials determined that the drone was likely struck by Ukrainian air defenses over Ukraine, which altered its trajectory before it entered Romanian airspace. The impact hit the roof of the residential building in Galati, which sits on the Danube River west of the borders with Moldova and Ukraine.

The incident prompted swift action from Romania's government. President Dan convened an emergency meeting of the country's supreme council of national defence, and the foreign ministry summoned Russia's ambassador. Romania's foreign minister, Oana Toiu, said the country would formally communicate the consequences for diplomatic relations with Russia and discuss next steps regarding European Union sanctions. She described the incident as a "grave and irresponsible escalation" and a serious breach of international law.

Romania requested that NATO accelerate the transfer of anti-drone capabilities to the country. The government also indicated it would invoke Article 4 of the NATO treaty, which triggers formal discussions within the alliance about threats to a member's security.

General Gheorghe Maxim, a stand-in commander for Romania's armed forces, clarified that the strike was not "an attack from Russia against Romania," but emphasized that Romanians should understand Russia poses a threat to regional security.

Russia denied responsibility for the incident. President Vladimir Putin suggested the drone wreckage should be handed over to Russia for an independent investigation, claiming he had only recently learned of the incident.

The European Union and France also condemned the strike. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Russia's "war of aggression has crossed yet another line" and pledged full solidarity with Romania. France's foreign minister called it an irresponsible act by Russia.

Ukraine's foreign minister said the incident demonstrated that Russian aggression poses a threat to the entire European region. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has been pressing the United States to provide additional Patriot air defense missiles to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks, as Russia intensifies its campaign against Ukraine.

The Romanian military scrambled two F-16 fighter jets and a helicopter in response to the incident.

cards.teaser: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the country is preparing for significant Russian military operations in the coming day.

cards.headline: School Fire Kills 16 Students in Kenya
cards.teaser: Kenyan authorities arrested eight students after a dormitory fire at a police-run school killed 16 people.
cards.body:
A fire broke out just after midnight at Utumishi girls academy in Gilgil, Nakuru county, about 76 miles northwest of Nairobi, killing at least 16 students. The blaze tore through a dormitory at the girls' school located in Kenya's Rift Valley.

Following the incident, Kenya's education minister said eight students were arrested. The students could face charges next week, though authorities have not disclosed the specific charges or the cause of the fire.

cards.headline: Man Admits Aiding Suicides by Selling Toxic Chemicals Online
cards.teaser: Kenneth Law pleaded guilty to charges related to selling toxic chemicals to people across multiple countries.
cards.body:
Kenneth Law, a Canadian man, has pleaded guilty to 14 counts of assisting suicide. He mailed packages containing lethal chemicals and instructions to more than 100 people across multiple countries, including Canada, the UK, the US, Italy, Australia and New Zealand. Prosecutors withdrew 14 murder charges as part of a plea agreement. Sentencing is expected in September.

Families of victims in Britain are calling for Law to face charges in the UK, where 79 deaths have been linked to his actions. So far, he has only been charged in connection with Canadian victims.

cards.headline: Ghana Lawmakers Pass Bill Criminalizing LGBTQ Activity
cards.teaser: Ghana's parliament approved legislation that criminalizes the promotion of LGBTQ rights and identities.
cards.body:
Ghana's parliament has approved legislation that criminalizes LGBTQ promotion and activity. The bill now requires the president's signature to become law.

The measure was passed ahead of a scheduled anti-gay conference and has gained international attention as among Africa's most restrictive laws targeting LGBTQ people.

cards.headline: Mexico Moves to Allow Voiding Elections Over Foreign Interference
cards.teaser: The Mexican Senate voted to permit the cancellation of elections if foreign interference is detected.
cards.body:
Mexico's Senate has passed a constitutional amendment that would allow election results to be annulled if foreign interference is proven to have affected the outcome. President Claudia Sheinbaum presented the bill, which defines foreign interference to include illicit financing, propaganda, misinformation campaigns, digital manipulation, and intervention by foreign governments or agencies.

The legislation now requires approval from a majority of state legislatures before advancing to the president. Opposition groups have raised alarm about the measure, arguing it could give the ruling party unchecked power to overturn election results and override the will of voters.

hero.headline: Judge orders Trump's name removed from Kennedy Center
hero.teaser: A federal judge ruled that Trump cannot add his name to the Kennedy Center and blocked planned renovations that would close the arts venue.
hero.body:
A federal judge ordered the removal of Donald Trump's name from the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, ruling that the venue cannot be renamed without an act of Congress. US District Judge Christopher Cooper directed the Trump administration to remove all physical signage bearing Trump's name and eliminate references to a "Trump Kennedy Center" from official materials within 14 days.

The ruling also blocked the Trump administration's plan to close the performing arts center for two years of renovations. The judge wrote in his 94-page decision that it was "crystal clear" the arts complex was named for President John F. Kennedy.

cards.headline: Five killed in bus crash on Interstate 95 in Virginia
cards.teaser: A bus crashed into six cars on I-95 in Stafford County, Virginia, killing five people and injuring more than 30 others.
cards.body:
A collision involving a bus and multiple vehicles on Interstate 95 southbound in Stafford County claimed five lives. Children ages 13 and 7 were among those killed in the crash.

The incident resulted in more than 30 injuries, with 44 people transported to hospitals for medical treatment. The crash triggered a major emergency response on the heavily-traveled interstate corridor.

cards.headline: ICE agent charged in Minneapolis shooting arrested in Texas
cards.teaser: An ICE officer wanted for shooting a man during immigration enforcement operations in Minneapolis was arrested in Texas.
cards.body:
Christian Castro, a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent, was arrested in Texas on Friday, 11 days after Minneapolis prosecutors charged him with assault and falsely reporting a crime. Castro was wanted in connection with the shooting of a Venezuelan man during immigration enforcement activities in Minneapolis.

The non-fatal shooting occurred in January during what ICE called Operation Metro Surge, a crackdown on undocumented immigrants in the Minneapolis area. Video footage of the incident emerged, leading to Castro's charges.

cards.headline: Kenyan court blocks U.S. plan to treat American Ebola patients in Africa
cards.teaser: A court in Kenya suspended a U.S. plan to establish a quarantine facility for American Ebola patients in the country.
cards.body:
A Kenyan court suspended the U.S. government's proposal to establish a quarantine facility in the country for American Ebola patients. The court's decision blocked the plan to house infected Americans in Africa rather than bringing them back to the United States.

The ruling represents a setback for the administration's strategy on managing Ebola cases among American citizens.

cards.headline: Teenager Joao Fonseca stuns Djokovic at French Open
cards.teaser: Novak Djokovic's pursuit of a record 25th Grand Slam title ended after teenage star Joao Fonseca came back to win a five-set match in the French Open third round.
cards.body:
Brazilian teenager Joao Fonseca defeated Novak Djokovic 4-6, 4-6, 6-3, 7-5, 7-5 in a five-set thriller during the French Open third round. Despite Djokovic commanding a two-set lead on Court Philippe-Chatrier, the 19-year-old mounted an impressive comeback to eliminate the tennis legend from the tournament.

The grueling four-hour match took its toll on the 39-year-old Djokovic, whose bid for a record 25th Grand Slam title continues. Fonseca's victory represents a significant upset, with the young Brazilian overpowering a vastly more experienced opponent.

cards.headline: California governor race could see two Democrats advance, new poll shows
cards.teaser: A new poll in California's gubernatorial race indicates a slim but growing possibility that two Democratic candidates could advance to the general election.
cards.body:
A new poll suggests California's gubernatorial race could result in two Democratic candidates advancing to the general election under the state's top-two primary system. Becerra leads the crowded field of candidates vying to replace Governor Newsom.

The polling data indicates Democrats maintain strong positions in the race, though the possibility of two Democrats advancing remains narrow but appears to be growing based on the latest survey results.

cards.teaser: Major stock indexes closed at record levels, with technology companies leading gains and the Nasdaq rising 8% for May.
cards.body:
Wall Street reached new closing highs as technology stocks led the advance. The Nasdaq climbed 8% during May, while the S&P 500 extended its winning streak to nine consecutive weeks.

The market rally reflected investor optimism about technology companies and corporate earnings growth. Positive sentiment was further bolstered by hopes for a diplomatic agreement between the U.S. and Iran regarding Middle East developments.

cards.headline: Oil heads for biggest monthly decline since 2020
cards.teaser: Crude oil prices are on track for their steepest monthly drop in six years as diplomatic progress eases Middle East tensions.
cards.body:
Oil prices are on track for their biggest monthly decline since 2020, with Brent crude futures down 19% since the end of April. The global benchmark was trading around $92 on Friday, down 1.3% that day. Hopes for a U.S.-Iran peace deal have driven the sharp decline in energy costs.

The steep monthly drop reflects investor optimism about a potential end to tensions in the region. Stock markets have rallied as crude prices eased, providing relief from elevated energy costs that had weighed on sentiment.

cards.headline: Blue Origin rocket explodes during ground test at Cape Canaveral
cards.teaser: A Blue Origin rocket exploded during ground testing at Launch Complex 36, creating a setback for the company and NASA's moon program.
cards.body:
A Blue Origin New Glenn rocket exploded during a hotfire test at Cape Canaveral in Florida on Thursday night. The massive fireball destroyed the launch pad at Kennedy Space Center, with the orange glow visible over 115 miles away in Fort Pierce. No personnel were harmed in the incident, which the company described as an anomaly.

The explosion threatens NASA's lunar exploration timeline. Blue Origin has contracts supporting the agency's moon program, and the setback jeopardizes plans to build a lunar base and return humans to the moon within the next two years.

cards.headline: Universal Music Group rejects Bill Ackman's $64 billion takeover offer
cards.teaser: The music company turned down Pershing Square's bid, saying it fundamentally undervalues the business.
cards.body:
Universal Music Group has rejected billionaire investor Bill Ackman's $64 billion acquisition proposal through his firm Pershing Square, stating the offer significantly undervalues the company. Shareholders supported management's decision to decline the bid.

The rejection represents a setback for Ackman's effort to acquire the music industry giant, which manages major recording artists and controls extensive music catalogs.

cards.headline: UnitedHealthcare to eliminate prior authorization for most pediatric services
cards.teaser: The insurer will remove approval requirements for nearly two-thirds of children's medical services.
cards.body:
UnitedHealthcare announced it will remove insurance prior approval requirements for some pediatric services. The change will eliminate authorization requirements for nearly two-thirds of pediatric services, representing a significant shift in how the company processes children's medical care requests.

The decision affects a wide range of pediatric medical services that previously required advance insurer approval before treatment could proceed. UnitedHealth's policy change aims to streamline access to children's healthcare services by reducing administrative requirements for providers and families seeking medical care for minors.

cards.headline: NextEra Energy's political influence in Florida scrutinized ahead of Dominion acquisition
cards.teaser: The utility company has clashed with consumer groups, residents, and journalists while seeking regulatory approval for its Dominion Energy purchase.
cards.body:
NextEra Energy's political power in Florida is facing examination as the company pursues its acquisition of Dominion Energy. NextEra has frequently butted heads with consumer groups, residents, and journalists in its home state.

The company's political activities in Florida have drawn attention as regulators consider the proposed Dominion Energy purchase. NextEra's track record of engagement with stakeholders and media in Florida provides context for understanding how the company might operate if the acquisition proceeds. The utility's approach to navigating political and regulatory environments has become a factor in evaluating the merger.

hero.headline: Botnet of more than 17 million devices dismantled
hero.body:
Authorities dismantled a botnet comprising more than 17 million devices, marking one of the largest takedowns of its kind. The operation targeted infrastructure used to control the massive network of compromised computers and other internet-connected devices.

The botnet was tied to a Russia-based residential proxy network, according to reports. Residential proxy networks route internet traffic through compromised home devices, often without the knowledge of the device owners. This allows malicious actors to mask their online activities by making them appear to originate from legitimate residential IP addresses.

Botnets of this scale are typically used for various criminal activities, including distributed denial-of-service attacks, credential stuffing, web scraping, and ad fraud. The use of residential devices makes detection and prevention more challenging, as traffic appears to come from ordinary home internet connections rather than data centers or known malicious sources.

The sheer size of this botnet, with more than 17 million compromised devices, represents a significant threat to internet security. Each infected device can be remotely controlled to carry out coordinated attacks or other malicious activities. Device owners often remain unaware their equipment has been compromised until they notice performance issues or receive notifications from their internet service providers.

The dismantling operation likely involved coordination between multiple law enforcement agencies and cybersecurity organizations. Such takedowns typically require identifying and seizing command-and-control servers that manage the botnet, as well as working with internet service providers to notify affected users and help clean infected devices.

The connection to a Russia-based operation follows a pattern of large-scale cybercrime infrastructure originating from or operating through Russian networks. Residential proxy networks have become increasingly popular among cybercriminals because they provide a veneer of legitimacy to malicious traffic and are harder to block than traditional proxy services.

cards.headline: Kenyan court blocks Trump administration plan to send Ebola-exposed Americans to Kenya
cards.teaser: A Kenyan court blocked the Trump administration from sending Americans exposed to Ebola to Kenya for quarantine.
cards.body:
A Kenyan court has blocked the Trump administration's plan to quarantine Americans exposed to Ebola in Kenya. The White House had confirmed it was building a quarantine and treatment facility in Kenya for US citizens who had exposure to Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, rather than bringing them back to the United States.

Some health experts have criticized the administration's approach, arguing that preventing Americans from returning home undermines treatment efforts for the outbreak.

cards.headline: Samsung Display develops first 4K 360Hz OLED panel for gaming monitors
cards.teaser: Samsung Display created the world's first OLED panel capable of displaying 4K resolution at 360Hz refresh rate.
cards.body:
Samsung Display announced it developed the world's first 4K 360Hz OLED panel, advancing display technology for gaming monitors. The quantum dot OLED panel combines ultra-high resolution with extremely fast refresh rates, addressing two key performance metrics for gaming displays.

MSI plans to debut a gaming monitor using the new panel technology at Computex. The monitor will feature a triple-mode capability, allowing users to switch between 4K at 360Hz, 1440p at 520Hz, and 1080p at 680Hz depending on their performance needs. Samsung also announced improvements to brightness levels in the new QD-OLED panels.

cards.headline: Analysis of Texas measles outbreak shows hospitalization rate near 20 percent
cards.teaser: An analysis of a Texas measles outbreak found roughly one in five cases required hospitalization.
cards.body:
An analysis of a measles outbreak in Texas revealed that approximately one in five infected individuals required hospitalization. The hospitalization rate underscores the severity of measles infections and the medical care often needed to manage the disease.

Most of the hospitalized patients developed complications from the measles infection. Measles can lead to serious health problems including pneumonia, encephalitis, and other conditions that require intensive medical treatment. The outbreak data provides evidence of the virus's danger to public health.

cards.headline: FCC warns broadcasters to comply with orders following ABC license action
cards.teaser: The FCC under Trump warned all broadcasters to follow commission orders or face consequences similar to ABC.
cards.body:
The Federal Communications Commission issued a warning to all broadcasters to comply with FCC orders or face enforcement action similar to recent measures taken against ABC. The warning came from the agency under the Trump administration, signaling potential regulatory scrutiny across the broadcast industry.

ABC responded that the early renewal process for all of its stations was unprecedented and served no legitimate regulatory purpose. The network contested the FCC's actions as departing from standard licensing procedures used for broadcast stations.

cards.headline: Justice Department sues states that refused ICE undercover license plate requests
cards.teaser: The Justice Department filed lawsuits against states that rejected requests from ICE for undercover license plates.
cards.body:
The Justice Department initiated legal action against multiple states that declined to provide Immigration and Customs Enforcement with undercover license plates. The lawsuits target states that refused to comply with ICE requests for unmarked vehicle registration.

The Justice Department has repeatedly accused websites that monitor ICE activities of doxing agents, though evidence supporting these claims remains limited. The legal push for undercover plates comes amid broader debates over immigration enforcement and transparency in federal law enforcement operations.

cards.headline: Google rolls out Gemini Spark AI agent to Ultra subscribers in US
cards.teaser: Google began rolling out Gemini Spark, an AI agent feature, to Google AI Ultra subscribers in the United States.
cards.body:
Google started deploying Gemini Spark to subscribers of its Google AI Ultra service in the United States. The AI agent represents an expansion of Google's artificial intelligence offerings to paying customers.

The Gemini Mac app will receive the Spark agent feature during summer 2026. Google also announced nine new features as part of its Gemini Drops update for the month, expanding the capabilities available to users of its AI platform.

hero.headline: 19-year-old Fonseca rallies from two sets down to upset Djokovic at French Open
hero.body:
Novak Djokovic's pursuit of a record 25th Grand Slam singles title came to an end in the third round of the French Open when Brazilian teenager Joao Fonseca mounted a remarkable comeback to claim victory in five sets.

Fonseca, 19, won 4-6, 4-6, 6-3, 7-5, 7-5 after nearly five hours of play on Court Philippe-Chatrier. The match lasted four hours and 53 minutes, with Fonseca refusing to surrender despite Djokovic's commanding two-set advantage. The 39-year-old Serbian champion, who holds 24 Grand Slam titles, could not maintain his early dominance on the red clay courts of Roland Garros.

The physical and mental toll of the match became evident as Djokovic struggled in the later stages. After four hours of intense competition, the champion's body showed signs of fatigue. Djokovic's two-set lead gradually unraveled as Fonseca's aggressive play and powerful serving took control of the contest. The Brazilian teenager demonstrated remarkable composure under pressure, winning three consecutive sets to complete an unexpected upset.

Fonseca's comeback ranks among the most impressive in recent Grand Slam history. This was only his second five-set match ever, yet he showed no signs of fatigue or mental weakness as the match progressed. His serving proved particularly effective in the final sets, with the teenager hitting multiple aces when it mattered most. When asked how he believed he could win from two sets down, Fonseca responded: "I didn't, really. It's my first time stepping on court with [Djokovic], he's a legend... I'm just really happy."

The teenager explained that as daylight faded during the match, the court conditions slowed down, which aided his comeback. "I wasn't thinking about [the occasion], I was just trying to hit the ball as hard as I could," Fonseca said. He also credited his powerful serving, noting: "I felt like John Isner [hitting three aces] – I had no idea I could hit them like this."

Fonseca's victory becomes only the second time in tennis history that a player has defeated Djokovic after trailing two sets to nothing. The only previous instance came against Jürgen Melzer at the 2010 French Open, when Fonseca was just three years old.

With this breakthrough win, Fonseca joins a growing generation of young players challenging tennis's established dominance. The teenager's next opponent will be either Casper Ruud or Tommy Paul in the fourth round.

Djokovic's early exit eliminates a tournament favorite and extends his wait for what would be a historic 25th major singles title, breaking his current tie with Margaret Court for the most Grand Slam singles championships in tennis history.

cards.headline: Anthony Gordon completes transfer from Newcastle to Barcelona
cards.teaser: Barcelona signed Newcastle United winger Anthony Gordon in a deal worth more than 69.3 million pounds.
cards.body:
Anthony Gordon has completed his transfer from Newcastle United to Barcelona in a deal worth £69.3 million. The 25-year-old English winger has signed a five-year contract with the Spanish champions, keeping him at the club until June 2031.

Gordon expressed his delight at joining Barcelona, describing the move as a dream he has held since childhood. The winger will now compete for playing time in Barcelona's attacking ranks as they pursue further success in La Liga.

cards.headline: Pittsburgh Steelers fire assistant special teams coach Derius Swinton II
cards.teaser: The Steelers dismissed assistant special teams coach Derius Swinton II after just three months on the job.
cards.body:
The Pittsburgh Steelers fired assistant special teams coach Derius Swinton II months into his tenure with the team. Multiple reports indicated the dismissal resulted from a violation of club policy.

Swinton had been on the job for approximately three months before his dismissal. The Steelers have not provided additional details about the nature of the policy violation that led to his firing.

cards.headline: Bristol beats defending champion Bath to keep playoff hopes alive
cards.teaser: Bristol defeated reigning Premiership champions Bath 21-19 to maintain their chances of reaching the playoffs.
cards.body:
Bristol kept their playoff hopes alive with a hard-fought 21-19 victory over Bath. The West Country rivals produced a tense encounter, with Bristol digging deep to secure the win against the reigning Premiership champions.

The narrow two-point margin demonstrated the competitive nature of the match. The victory gives Bristol a chance to gatecrash the playoff places as they continue their push for a top-four finish.

cards.headline: Glasgow Warriors advance to United Rugby Championship semifinals
cards.teaser: Glasgow Warriors defeated Connacht and will face either Bulls or Munster in the United Rugby Championship semifinals.
cards.body:
Glasgow Warriors have secured a place in the United Rugby Championship semi-finals with a hard-fought victory over Connacht. The Scottish side will now await their opponent in the next round.

Glasgow's semifinal opponent will be determined by the result of the Bulls versus Munster quarterfinal match.

cards.headline: Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart addresses team after Trump introduction
cards.teaser: New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart spoke with teammates after introducing President Trump at an event.
cards.body:
Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart held a meeting with his team to discuss his introduction of President Trump. Dart described the opportunity as unique, while teammate Abdul Carter also shared his viewpoint on the matter.

The meeting came after some disagreement within the team regarding Dart's role in introducing the president. Both Dart and defensive player Abdul Carter later expressed their perspectives publicly, with the two players working to address the situation with their teammates.

cards.headline: Boxing promoter Eddie Hearn challenges Dana White to release UFC fighter Tom Aspinall
cards.teaser: Eddie Hearn proposed that UFC president Dana White release heavyweight fighter Tom Aspinall from his contract.
cards.body:
Boxing promoter Eddie Hearn publicly challenged UFC president Dana White to release heavyweight fighter Tom Aspinall from his UFC contract. Hearn offered to walk away from a legal situation involving boxer Conor Benn if White would release Aspinall.

Hearn criticized what he described as low pay for Aspinall under his current UFC deal. The promoter characterized Aspinall's contract as one of the worst in sports and suggested the fighter would be better served competing outside the UFC.

hero.headline: More Than Half of Great American State Fair Performers Withdraw Over Politics and Threats
hero.body:
More than half of the scheduled performers for the Great American State Fair have withdrawn from the event, citing political concerns and threats. The fair is part of the Freedom 250 concert series, which was designed to celebrate the nation's 250th anniversary.

Several high-profile artists have pulled out of the lineup in recent weeks. Bret Michaels, the frontman of the band Poison, became one of the latest performers to cancel his appearance. Country music artist Martina McBride also joined the growing number of cancellations from the Trump-linked Freedom 250 concerts scheduled to take place on the National Mall in Washington.

The Freedom 250 concert series was planned as a centerpiece of the broader 250th anniversary celebration for the United States. The events are being held on the National Mall and were intended to draw major musical talent to the festivities.

The withdrawals appear to be driven by the political nature of the event and concerns about safety. Multiple performers have cited these factors as reasons for stepping back from their scheduled performances. The association between the concert series and the Trump administration seems to have influenced several artists' decisions to decline participation in the anniversary celebration.

The scale of the cancellations has raised significant questions about the future of the event. With more than half of the originally scheduled performers now pulling out, organizers face the challenge of maintaining the planned scope and quality of the Great American State Fair programming.

As of now, organizers have not publicly announced plans to bring in replacement performers or explained how the withdrawals will affect the overall structure of the Freedom 250 concert series. The uncertainty surrounding the event continues to grow as additional artists choose not to participate.

The situation highlights the increasingly polarized landscape around high-profile public events. Artists are weighing the professional opportunities and visibility that come with performing at a major national celebration against concerns about the political implications of their participation. The threats and political pressure that some performers have reported add another layer of complexity to their decision-making process.

The anniversary celebration, which was meant to bring Americans together in a spirit of national pride and unity, has instead become a flashpoint for political division. The struggling lineup suggests that organizers may need to recalibrate their approach or expectations for the remaining Freedom 250 events.

The outcome of these concerts will likely be closely watched as a barometer of how political polarization continues to affect major American cultural and civic events. Whether organizers can salvage the event with a new lineup or whether additional cancellations are forthcoming remains to be seen.

cards.headline: Judge Blocks Trump From Adding Name to Kennedy Center
cards.teaser: A federal judge ruled that President Trump cannot add his name to the Kennedy Center building.
cards.body:
U.S. District Judge Casey Cooper ruled that the Kennedy Center cannot be formally renamed or bear a public memorial based solely on the board's decision. Trump had ordered his name placed on the building as part of planned renovations, but the judge blocked this action. The 94-page ruling emphasized that the arts complex is formally named for the late President John F. Kennedy.

The judge also blocked Trump's plans to close the Kennedy Center for two years of extensive renovations, requiring the center to remain open. Trump responded by criticizing the judge and announcing plans to transfer the institution to congressional control.

cards.headline: Backrooms Director Kane Parsons Discusses Film Opening in Theaters
cards.teaser: The 20-year-old director behind the web series Backrooms saw his feature film adaptation open through A24.
cards.body:
Kane Parsons, the 20-year-old filmmaker behind the Backrooms web series, directed the feature film adaptation now playing in theaters through A24. Parsons expressed concern that his vision might be altered during production, though the film has performed strongly in preview screenings and is projected to be one of A24's biggest releases.

In interviews, Parsons discussed his approach to depicting liminal spaces on screen and outlined potential directions for future sequels.

cards.headline: Judge Reinstates Defamation Judgment Against Blogger in Megan Thee Stallion Case
cards.teaser: A court ruling found that blogger Milagro Gramz was commissioned by Tory Lanez's family to call Megan Thee Stallion a liar.
cards.body:
A judge reinstated a defamation judgment against blogger Milagro Gramz in her case involving rapper Megan Thee Stallion. The court determined that Gramz was commissioned by Tory Lanez's family to make statements branding Megan a liar.

The ruling found that Gramz does not qualify for media defendant protections typically afforded to journalists and publishers. Because she was acting on behalf of Lanez's family rather than as an independent media entity, she lost those legal protections for the statements she made about Megan Thee Stallion.

cards.headline: Beastie Boys Former Studio Launches Fundraiser to Reopen as Music Venue
cards.teaser: G-Son Studios in Los Angeles is raising money through Kickstarter to become a community arts center and concert space.
cards.body:
G-Son Studios, the former rehearsal space, recording studio, and headquarters of the Beastie Boys, launched a public fundraising campaign on Kickstarter. The initiative aims to restore and reopen the facility as a community arts center and live music venue.

The studio is located in the Atwater Village neighborhood of Los Angeles. The building was previously a ballroom before the Beastie Boys converted it into their creative headquarters and recording facility.

cards.headline: Hannah Einbinder Criticizes Spencer Pratt's Mayoral Campaign
cards.teaser: The Hacks actress spoke out against Spencer Pratt's run for mayor of Los Angeles after the show's finale.
cards.body:
Following the series finale of Hacks, Hannah Einbinder spoke out against Spencer Pratt's bid to become Los Angeles mayor. She emphasized the importance of opposing his candidacy.

Einbinder highlighted the concentration of wealth in Los Angeles, noting that many residents present themselves as Democrats or progressives while being primarily driven by financial interests.

cards.headline: Kardashian Family Seeks Protection Order Against Man Allegedly Obsessed With Kylie
cards.teaser: The Kardashians are pursuing legal protection against an individual they say is fixated on Kylie Jenner.
cards.body:
The Kardashian family is seeking a protection order against a man who is allegedly obsessed with Kylie Jenner. TMZ reported that the family filed for legal action to keep the individual away from the family members.

The nature of the alleged obsession and specific incidents that prompted the protection request were reported by TMZ. The family is using legal channels to address safety concerns related to the individual's behavior toward Kylie.

hero.headline: Judge orders Trump's name removed from Kennedy Center, halts closure
hero.body:
A federal judge has ordered that President Trump's name be removed from the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts and blocked the venue from closing for planned renovations.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled Friday that the performing arts center's board exceeded its authority when it voted to rename the institution. In his 94-page decision, Cooper wrote that it was "crystal clear" the arts complex has been named for the late President John F. Kennedy since 1964, when Congress officially redesignated it as the "John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts."

The ruling sided with Rep. Joyce Beatty, a Democrat from Ohio and an ex officio member of the center's board, who challenged the renaming. Cooper concluded the board lacked the statutory power to make such a change without broader authorization.

"The Court has concluded that the Board overstepped its statutory bounds by unilaterally renaming the Kennedy Center after President Trump," Cooper wrote in his decision.

The order requires the Trump administration to remove all signage bearing Trump's name from the building and to eliminate any references to a "Trump Kennedy Center" from official materials within 14 days. The decision takes effect immediately.

The ruling also blocks the Kennedy Center's planned closure later this year. The venue was scheduled to shut down so extensive renovations could begin, with programming expected to wind down over a two-year construction period.

The decision represents a significant setback to the administration's renovation plans for the performing arts venue. Trump had pushed for the changes as part of his broader vision for the facility.

The Kennedy Center, located in Washington, D.C., has functioned as the nation's cultural center since its opening. The building was designated as a living memorial to President Kennedy, who championed the arts during his administration.

Beatty brought the legal challenge in her capacity as a board member, arguing that renaming the institution violated the center's founding charter and federal law. The judge agreed with this assessment.

The order prevents any further steps toward closing the facility or advancing renovation plans under the current proposal. However, the ruling does not prevent Congress from potentially authorizing the renovation project or approving a different approach to the facility's future.

The decision comes after months of litigation surrounding the center's status and the administration's authority to make changes to the institution. Judge Cooper had previously signaled concerns about the board's actions during earlier proceedings in the case.

cards.headline: Detention facility in New Jersey tests new DHS secretary
cards.teaser: Protesters have been arrested outside Delaney Hall as detainees reportedly participate in a hunger strike over living conditions.
cards.body:
A private detention center in New Jersey has become a flashpoint in the Trump administration's immigration policies, testing new Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. The Delaney Hall Facility in Newark has been the site of protests and reports of a hunger strike by detainees citing inhumane conditions and inadequate medical care.

New Jersey state officials announced they will take over policing operations at the facility from federal immigration officers. Governor Mikie Sherrill and Attorney General Jennifer Davenport said state police will establish a "peaceful protected zone" for demonstrators at the site, as reports indicate an influx of federal agents arriving at the facility.

cards.headline: Bulgaria to end US military aircraft presence over visa dispute
cards.teaser: The Bulgarian prime minister said US military aircraft will leave Sofia at the end of June after visa program negotiations stalled.
cards.body:
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev announced Friday that his country will terminate the deployment of U.S. military aircraft in Sofia by the end of June. The decision stems from the Trump administration's rejection of visa-free travel for Bulgarian citizens to the United States.

Radev stated he had raised the visa suspension issue during discussions with U.S. officials. The dispute marks a significant disagreement between the two NATO allies over immigration policy.

cards.headline: Former Iowa schools chief sentenced to two years on immigration, gun charges
cards.teaser: Ian Roberts, who led Des Moines schools, pleaded guilty to falsely claiming citizenship and illegally possessing a firearm.
cards.body:
Ian Roberts, the former school superintendent of Des Moines, Iowa, was sentenced Friday to two years in prison after pleading guilty to federal charges. He admitted to falsely claiming to be a U.S. citizen and illegally possessing a firearm.

Roberts had led one of the state's largest school districts, which serves more than 30,000 students, from 2023 until his legal troubles emerged. The case involved both immigration violations and weapons charges brought by federal prosecutors.

cards.headline: Former Attorney General Bondi addresses Epstein files handling
cards.teaser: Pam Bondi appeared before officials to discuss missteps in the handling of Epstein-related documents.
cards.body:
Former Attorney General Pam Bondi testified before Congress regarding errors in handling Jeffrey Epstein-related files. During the closed-door hearing, Bondi acknowledged "redaction errors" in the documents while defending the Justice Department's overall approach to the case.

Bondi characterized the department's record under her leadership as reflecting an "unprecedented commitment to transparency" in managing the Epstein materials. The testimony occurred roughly a month after she was removed from office by President Trump.

cards.headline: Jill Biden discusses husband's cancer diagnosis
cards.teaser: The former first lady called the prostate cancer diagnosis shocking in a new interview.
cards.body:
Former first lady Jill Biden spoke with CBS News about her husband's prostate cancer diagnosis, which he announced in May of the previous year. In a preview clip released Friday, she described the diagnosis as shocking and expressed surprise that it had not been detected earlier.

The interview marks one of the first occasions when Jill Biden has publicly discussed the personal impact of the former president's health battle. A spokesperson had previously provided details about his treatment at the time of the announcement.

cards.headline: FAA head says air traffic system runs on outdated technology
cards.teaser: The administrator said the system is safe but operates on computing power from the 1970s and 1980s.
cards.body:
Federal Aviation Administration Administrator Bryan Bedford said Friday that while the nation's air traffic control infrastructure is safe, it operates on decades-old technology that needs improvement. Bedford noted the system still runs on 1970s and 1980s computing power and compact disks.

Bedford said there is real reliability risk in the system because of the outdated equipment. He called the current state of the technology infrastructure concerning, despite maintaining that safety standards remain intact.
